cues.text: Section four: IT budgeting and financial planning.
A budget forecasts and allocates money for technology operations and initiatives.
Financial planning looks further ahead.
It considers longer-term needs, cash flow, risks and business strategy.
Alongside both, cost management monitors and controls expenditure.
Now let us separate two kinds of spending.
Capital expenditure, or CapEx, is spending on assets that are expected to provide benefits over multiple periods, subject to accounting recognition rules.
Operational expenditure, or OpEx, is spending recognised as an operating expense, such as recurring subscriptions and support.
Buying servers is commonly CapEx, while monthly cloud consumption is commonly OpEx.
But be careful: the accounting treatment depends on the contract and the applicable standards, and not every software purchase is capitalisable.
Next, depreciation and amortisation.
Depreciation allocates the cost of a tangible asset over its useful life.
Amortisation performs a similar function for qualifying intangible assets.
Neither is identical to cash expenditure.
Consider an example.
A server costs ₦12m, has a three-year useful life and zero residual value.
Using straight-line depreciation, the annual charge is ₦4m, that is ₦12m divided by three years, even though the cash may have been paid upfront.
Now the budgeting cycle.
It includes strategic planning, requirements gathering, cost estimation, prioritisation, approval, execution, monitoring and review.
There are several budgeting approaches.
Incremental budgeting adjusts the previous budget.
Zero-based budgeting requires justification of expenditure.
Rolling forecasts update estimates as circumstances change.
There is also a difference in direction: top-down budgeting sets limits from leadership, while bottom-up budgeting aggregates estimates from teams.
Good budgeting depends on forecasting.
Forecast demand, staffing, licensing, exchange rates, inflation and infrastructure growth.
Scenario planning compares plausible outcomes.
For example, a cloud service budgeted at ₦10m may cost ₦12m if usage or currency costs increase by 20%, assuming other factors stay constant.
For this reason, reserve contingency for uncertainty, rather than treating estimates as guaranteed.
Finally, measuring performance against the plan.
Budget variance equals actual expenditure minus budgeted expenditure.
If actual cost is ₦12m against a ₦10m budget, the adverse variance is ₦2m, or 20% of the budget.
When this happens, investigate whether the cause is price, usage, scope or forecasting error.
